opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the trickiest parts of the whole project. The core idea behind the time horizon work is that we want a single, interpretable axis for how capable these systems are, and we use how long a task takes a skilled human professional as a proxy for difficulty. But that only works if the tasks actually measure something real, and not just whether the model has seen something similar before.

So a few principles guide how we build them.

First, we try to make tasks that are novel in their specifics even if they're familiar in kind. A software engineering task might involve a pretty standard skill, like debugging or implementing a feature, but we set it in a codebase or environment we've constructed ourselves, with idiosyncratic details you couldn't have memorized. The model has to read, explore, form hypotheses, and act. It can't just pattern-match to a solution it's seen on GitHub.

Second, we care a lot about contamination. We keep many tasks private, we avoid putting solutions online, and we're thoughtful about which tasks we discuss publicly. If a task leaks into training data, it stops measuring generalization and starts measuring recall.

Third, and this is the subtler part, longer tasks are naturally harder to memorize. A five-minute task might really be one or two moves, and it's plausible a model has seen something nearly identical. A task that takes a human expert eight hours involves a long chain of decisions, recovering from mistakes, noticing that your approach isn't working and backtracking. That compositional, extended structure is much harder to shortcut. So part of why time horizon is interesting is that as you move up the axis, you're increasingly probing agency and adaptation rather than retrieval.

Fourth, we try to make the scoring robust. Ideally success is automatically checkable, and we think hard about whether there are ways to "pass" without actually doing the thing, like exploiting the grader, hardcoding outputs, or reward hacking. We've definitely seen models find clever shortcuts, and every time that happens it's a reminder that the task design itself is part of the measurement.

That said, I want to be honest about the limitations. Our tasks skew toward software and research engineering, partly because those are tractable to build and score, and partly because they're relevant to questions about AI accelerating AI research. Whether the trends we see transfer to messier, less well-specified real-world work is an open question. Real jobs have ambiguous goals, coordination with other people, and feedback that comes slowly. Our tasks are cleaner than that, so I'd treat the time horizon numbers as meaningful but not as a complete picture of what these systems can do in the wild.

r001.rationale: The response proposes familiar task types, such as debugging, in a custom codebase with idiosyncratic details that prevent reusing memorized solutions.

r002.rationale: It does not propose inferring an unknown black box’s function through interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the first thing I'd say is that "generalize beyond their training data" is doing a lot of work in that question, and when we were putting together the time horizon tasks at METR, we tried to be pretty disciplined about what we actually meant by it.

The core idea is that we want tasks where the difficulty scales with how long a human expert would take to do them, not with how obscure the knowledge is. Those are really different axes. You can make a task hard by asking about some niche fact that's underrepresented on the web, and a model will fail, but that tells you almost nothing about capability in the sense we care about. It tells you about coverage. What we actually want to know is: can the model sustain coherent, goal-directed work over a long stretch, recover from its own mistakes, notice when a sub-approach isn't working, and keep the overall objective in view? Those are the things that don't come for free from memorizing more text.

So in practice a few design principles fall out of that. One is that we baseline everything with humans who have the relevant expertise and are given the same environment the model gets. Not a guess at how long it would take, actual measured time. That's expensive and annoying, but without it the whole "horizon" framing is meaningless. You end up with a distribution of tasks spanning from a few minutes up to many hours, and the question becomes at what human-time length does the model's success rate cross fifty percent.

Another is that the tasks need to be things where there's genuinely no shortcut in the training distribution. A lot of software engineering benchmarks have this problem where the repository is public, the issue is public, the fix is public, and you're partially measuring retrieval. We try to build tasks that are either novel compositions of skills or are set in environments the model couldn't have seen, so the only way through is actually doing the work. That's not perfectly achievable, and we try to be honest about contamination risk, but it's the target.

A third thing, which I think people underweight, is that long tasks are more diagnostic because errors compound. If you have a task with twenty dependent steps and the model is ninety-five percent reliable per step, it's going to fail most of the time. Short tasks mask that. So the horizon framing is partly just a way of making the measurement sensitive to reliability and self-correction rather than peak performance on an individual move.

And then the uncomfortable caveat, which I'd rather say myself than have someone else say it: this is a messy measurement. The tasks are mostly software and research-flavored, because that's what we can score automatically and that's what's most relevant to the risk models we care about. Whether a fifty percent horizon of a few hours on our suite translates to anything about, say, real-world agentic work in a messy organization is an open question. I think of it as a useful trend line more than a precise capability readout. The trend has been strikingly consistent, which is interesting, but I'd push back on anyone who reads a specific number off that curve as if it were a fact about the world rather than a fact about our tasks.

r001.rationale: The response suggests novel skill combinations or unseen environments to prevent retrieval, but does not propose familiar tasks with unusual constraints.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose inferring an unknown black box's function through interaction.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing to distinguish is task duration from generalization. A task that takes a human several hours might still be something a model has seen many versions of in training. So making tasks longer doesn’t, by itself, establish that you’re testing generalization.

What you’d ideally do is construct fresh tasks that require familiar skills in unfamiliar combinations. You might give the model a new codebase, for example, and ask it to implement a feature whose requirements force it to understand several interacting components. You want success to depend on working through the particular problem, rather than recognizing a standard solution.

Then you need an outcome you can check independently, and a human baseline to estimate how long the task takes. That baseline is imperfect—different people have different experience—but it gives you a way to ask how reliability changes as the amount of work increases. I’d also want multiple tasks at each duration, because otherwise you can mistake difficulty in one particular domain for a limitation in time horizon.

And I’d be careful about the conclusion. Success on fresh tasks is evidence of generalization to those tasks. It isn’t proof that the model can handle arbitrary work of the same duration. The interesting question is whether that reliability carries across different settings, especially when the model has to maintain a plan, notice mistakes, and recover without someone intervening.

r001.rationale: The response proposes combining familiar skills in unfamiliar ways so success depends on solving the specific task rather than reusing a standard solution.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose inferring an unknown black box’s function through interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish a task taking a long time from a task actually requiring long-horizon reasoning. You can make something take hours just by adding repetitive work, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether a model can maintain a plan, notice mistakes, or recover when an assumption turns out to be wrong.

So you want tasks with dependencies: decisions early on affect what becomes possible later, and success requires integrating information across those steps. And then you want to vary the horizon while keeping other aspects of difficulty reasonably comparable. Otherwise, if performance drops, you don’t know whether that’s because the task is longer or because it requires some specialized knowledge.

For generalization, holding out the exact question isn’t enough. Ideally, you’re holding out some of the structure—new combinations of familiar skills, unfamiliar environments, or changed constraints—while still making the task well specified and objectively checkable.

And I’d look at more than the final success rate. Did the model make a sensible plan? Did it check its progress? Could it recover from an error? Those help distinguish a system that can reliably carry out an extended task from one that occasionally gets to the right answer.

r001.rationale: The response mentions new combinations and changed constraints, but does not clearly propose familiar tasks with unusual constraints that prevent reuse of standard solutions.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose inferring an unknown black box’s function through interaction.
